body.passage: Anna was nervous on her first day at the English club. She did not know how to start a conversation. Her teacher, Mr. Lee, smiled and said, "Don't worry. Let's learn some useful phrases today." First, they practiced greetings. "Hello, nice to meet you!" said Anna to a new friend. The friend smiled and answered, "Nice to meet you too!" Then Mr. Lee taught them how to ask for help politely. "Excuse me, could you repeat that, please?" Anna asked. Mr. Lee was happy and repeated the sentence slowly. At the end of the class, Anna felt much more confident. She said goodbye to her classmates: "It was great talking with you. See you next week!" On the bus home, Anna wrote the new phrases in her notebook. She decided to use one new phrase every day. Now, speaking English is not scary for her anymore.

examples.note: 'I think' + clause is the most common A2 way to give an opinion; adding 'but' lets you agree and refuse politely at the same time.

body.objective: Understand and use essential everyday speaking phrases for common A2 situations, including greetings, asking for repetition, giving opinions simply, and making polite requests, so the learner can manage basic spoken interactions with confidence.

explanation.en: At A2 level, spoken fluency depends less on complex grammar and more on having ready-made phrases you can use instantly. This topic covers four key groups of speaking phrases. (1) Greetings and small talk: 'How's it going?', 'Nice to see you!', 'How was your weekend?' – these open conversations naturally. (2) Asking for repetition or clarification: 'Sorry, could you say that again?', 'What do you mean?', 'Can you speak more slowly, please?' – these keep a conversation going when you don't understand. (3) Giving simple opinions: 'I think...', 'In my opinion...', 'I agree / I don't agree.' – use 'I think' + a clause for the most natural, flexible option. (4) Polite requests and responses: 'Could you...?', 'Would you mind + -ing...?', and answers like 'Sure, no problem' or 'I'm afraid I can't.' Note that 'Could you...?' is more polite than 'Can you...?'. Fixed phrases should be learned as whole chunks, not word by word, because their grammar is often irregular (e.g., 'Would you mind opening the window?' uses an -ing form, not a base verb). Practice saying them aloud with natural rhythm and intonation so they come out automatically in conversation.
explanation.vi: Ở trình độ A2, khả năng nói trôi chảy phụ thuộc nhiều vào việc thuộc lòng các cụm từ có sẵn chứ không chỉ ngữ pháp phức tạp. Chủ đề này gồm 4 nhóm chính. (1) Chào hỏi và nói chuyện phiếm: 'How's it going?', 'Nice to see you!', 'How was your weekend?' – giúp mở đầu cuộc trò chuyện tự nhiên. (2) Hỏi lại khi chưa nghe rõ: 'Sorry, could you say that again?', 'What do you mean?', 'Can you speak more slowly, please?' – giúp duy trì cuộc hội thoại khi bạn không hiểu. (3) Đưa ý kiến đơn giản: 'I think...', 'In my opinion...', 'I agree / I don't agree.' – 'I think' + mệnh đề là cách tự nhiên và linh hoạt nhất. (4) Yêu cầu lịch sự và trả lời: 'Could you...?', 'Would you mind + V-ing...?', và các câu trả lời như 'Sure, no problem' hoặc 'I'm afraid I can't.' Lưu ý 'Could you...?' lịch sự hơn 'Can you...?'. Hãy học các cụm từ này như một khối trọn vẹn, không học từng từ, vì ngữ pháp của chúng thường đặc biệt (ví dụ: 'Would you mind opening the window?' dùng dạng V-ing chứ không phải động từ nguyên mẫu). Nên tập nói to với ngữ điệu tự nhiên để khi nói thật các cụm từ này bật ra một cách tự động.

common_mistakes.why: After 'Would you mind', the verb must take the -ing form, not the infinitive with 'to'. This is a fixed pattern that must be memorized as a chunk.
common_mistakes.right: Would you mind opening the window?
common_mistakes.wrong: Would you mind to open the window?

common_mistakes.why: 'Agree' is a verb in English, not an adjective, so it does not take the verb 'to be'. Say 'I agree' or 'I don't agree'.
